lead: A three-wire three-phase load has no neutral, so you cannot multiply one phase voltage by one phase current. Two wattmeters, wired into any two lines, solve the problem. Their current coils carry two line currents; their voltage coils measure the two line-to-line voltages referred to the third line. The sum of the two readings is the total real power, for a balanced or an unbalanced load. The difference gives the reactive power and the power factor when the load is balanced. Industry uses this method on motors, feeders and distribution panels because it needs only two meters and no neutral connection.
prereq: You need real and reactive power and balanced three-phase quantities.

blocks.text: The connection. A three-wire system has lines R, Y and B, and no neutral. Each wattmeter has a current coil (CC) and a voltage coil (VC). Put the CC of W1 in line R and the CC of W2 in line Y. Connect the VC of W1 between R and B; connect the VC of W2 between Y and B. Line B is the common reference. A wattmeter reads V I cos θ, where V is the RMS voltage across its VC, I is the RMS current through its CC, and θ is the angle between them. In this connection each meter sees a line-to-line voltage VL and a line current IL. The total real power is P = W1 + W2. This sum is correct for a balanced load and also for an unbalanced load, as long as the system has three wires. The two meters need not be in R and Y; any two lines work, with the third line as the common voltage reference.

sections.h3: Balanced load: where the 30° comes from

blocks.text: Let VL be the RMS line voltage and IL the RMS line current. Let φ be the angle by which each line current lags its phase voltage. In a balanced three-phase system each line-to-line voltage differs in phase from the corresponding phase voltage by 30° (see phasor diagrams). For W1, with CC in R and VC across R and B, the angle between VRB and IR is 30° − φ. For W2, with CC in Y and VC across Y and B, the angle is 30° + φ. Therefore W1 = VL IL cos(30° − φ) and W2 = VL IL cos(30° + φ). Add them: cos(30° − φ) + cos(30° + φ) = 2 cos 30° cos φ = √3 cos φ. So P = W1 + W2 = √3 VL IL cos φ. Subtract: W1 − W2 = 2 VL IL sin 30° sin φ = VL IL sin φ. The total reactive power is Q = √3 VL IL sin φ, so Q = √3 (W1 − W2) in VAR. The power-factor angle follows from tan φ = Q/P = √3 (W1 − W2) / (W1 + W2). The power factor is pf = cos φ. These equations use lagging φ as positive; for a leading load, φ is negative and the signs of Q and W1−W2 reverse.
Follow these steps for a measurement.

items: Check that the load is three-wire. A four-wire system with neutral needs three wattmeters or a different method.
Insert the current coils in any two lines. Connect each voltage coil from its own line to the third line.
Read W<sub>1</sub> and W<sub>2</sub> with their signs. The algebraic sum is P.

If one reading is negative, swap the two terminals of that meter's voltage coil. Read the magnitude, then restore the negative sign in your calculation. The true reading is the negative of the displayed value.
For a balanced load, compute tan φ, then φ, then pf = cos φ. Compute Q = √3(W<sub>1</sub>−W<sub>2</sub>) in VAR.

blocks.text: At φ = 60°, cos(30° + 60°) = cos 90° = 0, so W<sub>2</sub> reads zero and pf = 0.5. Below 0.5 pf, W<sub>2</sub> is negative. A negative reading does not mean the load is capacitive; it only says the power factor is below 0.5, lagging or leading. For a four-wire system, use three wattmeters, one per phase. A single wattmeter can also be switched to take both readings, but it is slower.

figure.caption: At φ = 60° the second meter reads zero; beyond that its reading is negative. Their sum stays positive and equals √3 V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos φ.

spec.aria: Two wattmeter readings plotted against load angle: at zero degrees they are equal, at sixty degrees the second falls to zero, and beyond sixty the second turns negative while their sum follows √3 cos φ.

examples.question: Two wattmeters in a balanced three-phase circuit read W<sub>1</sub> = 5.5 kW and W<sub>2</sub> = 2.5 kW. Find the total power, the power factor and the reactive power. Assume the load is lagging.
steps: Total real power: P = W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub> = 5.5 + 2.5 = 8.0 kW.
examples.answer: P = 8.0 kW, pf = 0.839 lagging, Q = 5.20 kVAR.
examples.check:
import math
W1 = 5.5
W2 = 2.5
P = W1 + W2
D = W1 - W2
tanphi = math.sqrt(3) * D / P
phi = math.degrees(math.atan(tanphi))
pf = math.cos(math.radians(phi))
Q = math.sqrt(3) * D
S = P / pf
Qcheck = math.sqrt(S * S - P * P)
print(round(P, 2))
print(round(tanphi, 4))
print(round(phi, 1))
print(round(pf, 3))
print(round(Q, 2))
print(round(S, 2))
print(round(Qcheck, 2))

traps: Using phase voltage V<sub>p</sub> instead of line voltage V<sub>L</sub> in W<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>L</sub> I<sub>L</sub> cos(30° − φ). The meter sees line-to-line voltage.
Dropping the √3 in tan φ = √3(W<sub>1</sub> − W<sub>2</sub>)/(W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub>).
Treating a negative reading as proof of a capacitive load. It only says the power factor is below 0.5.
Adding the magnitudes when one reading is negative. Use the algebraic sum; a swapped voltage coil reverses the sign.
Connecting the voltage coils to neutral in a three-wire system. The common point must be the third line.

quiz.q: In the two-wattmeter method, where are the current coils and voltage coils connected in a three-wire system?
quiz.a: Current coils go in any two lines, here R and Y. Each voltage coil goes from its own line to the third line: W<sub>1</sub> from R to B, W<sub>2</sub> from Y to B.

quiz.q: Why does W<sub>1</sub> + W<sub>2</sub> give the total real power even when the load is unbalanced?
quiz.a: The two meters together account for the instantaneous power in all three lines. The third line carries the return current, and its power is included through the two line-to-line voltage measurements. The sum is therefore the total real power.

quiz.q: Two wattmeters read W<sub>1</sub> = 4 kW and W<sub>2</sub> = 1 kW on a balanced lagging load. Find P, tan φ, φ, pf and Q.
At φ = 60° which wattmeter reads zero, and what is the power factor? What happens at φ = 70°?
quiz.a: W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>cos(30° + 60°) = 0. The power factor is cos 60° = 0.5. At 70°, W<sub>2</sub> = V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>cos 100° is negative.

quiz.q: A wattmeter reads −1.2 kW. After swapping its voltage-coil terminals it reads 1.2 kW. What is the true reading to use in the calculation?
quiz.a: The true reading is −1.2 kW. The swapped meter shows the magnitude only.

quiz.q: Why must the voltage coils be connected to the third line and not to neutral in a three-wire system?
quiz.a: A three-wire system has no neutral. The third line is the only common reference available, and the method is built on line-to-line voltages.

quiz.q: Two wattmeter readings are equal. What is the power factor? If their sum is zero, what is the power factor?
quiz.a: Equal readings mean cos(30° − φ) = cos(30° + φ), so φ = 0° and pf = 1. A zero sum means √3 V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> cos φ = 0, so φ = 90° and pf = 0; the readings are +0.5 V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub> and −0.5 V<sub>L</sub>I<sub>L</sub>.

beyond: Not for the exam. In substations, the two-wattmeter idea appears inside panel meters and power-quality analysers that compute P, Q and pf from two voltage and two current channels. Modern digital relays sample all three phases and use the same sum-and-difference algebra. Search for "two-wattmeter method", "Blondel's theorem" and "three-phase power quality". Instrument transformers let the same method work at 11 kV and 33 kV, where you cannot connect a meter directly.
